title: Meet the Mushaf
tagline: Colors, short vowels and the tiny marks you will see everywhere.
intro: Welcome! Before the big tajweed rules, let's get comfortable with the page itself: what the colors mean, what the small marks above and below the letters do, and how long a vowel lasts. Everything later builds on these seven small lessons.

lessons.title: Meet the Colors
lessons.meaning: The color code of the Mushaf
lessons.summary: Tajweed colors are little signposts: each color tells you which rule is at work on that letter.
explain: The text in this course is the Madinah Mushaf (Hafs 'an 'Asim), shown in the King Fahd Complex script. Letters that carry a tajweed rule are colored, so your eyes learn the rules before your tongue has to.

Gray letters are quiet or hidden. Blue letters are stretched (madd). Red letters echo (qalqalah). Orange, purple, pink, teal, green and sky-blue belong to the noon and meem rules. You will meet each color in its own lesson.
Do not memorize the colors now. Every lesson introduces its own color, and the Color Key flashcards train them gently.
how: Look at a verse and notice which letters are colored.
Read the verse aloud, slowly, letting each colored letter remind you of its rule.
Open the Color Key at any time to check what a color means.
tips: Longer madd means a deeper blue.

showcase.note: Gray: the connecting alifs and the silent lam. Blue: the long vowels.
Lots of blue: this verse is a madd workout, including the deep-blue necessary madd at the end.
Red: the echo (qalqalah) on the last letter.

cards.q: What does a colored letter in a tajweed Mushaf tell you?
cards.a: A tajweed rule applies to that letter, and the color tells you which rule.

cards.q: In this course, what does a gray letter usually mean?
cards.a: It is quiet or hidden: a connecting alif (hamzat al-wasl), the lam of a sun letter, or a silent letter.

cards.q: Which blue is the longest madd?
cards.a: The deepest blue. Natural madd (2 counts) is the lightest blue; necessary madd (6 counts) is the deepest.

lessons.title: Short Vowels (Harakat)
lessons.summary: Three tiny marks tell your voice which short vowel to use: a, i or u.
explain: Arabic letters are consonants. Short vowel marks, the harakat, give each one its sound.
Fathah is a small slanted line above a letter and makes an 'a' sound: بَ = ba.
Kasrah is a small slanted line below a letter and makes an 'i' sound: بِ = bi.
Dammah is a tiny waw-shaped mark above a letter and makes a 'u' sound: بُ = bu.
A short vowel lasts one count (one harakah): about the time it takes to open or close one finger at a calm, steady pace.
how: Say the consonant, then the vowel that is marked on it.
Keep every short vowel quick and clean. Do not stretch it.
tips: Fathah opens the mouth (a), kasrah relaxes the jaw into a small smile (i), dammah rounds the lips (u).
mistakes: Stretching a short vowel until ba sounds like baa.

examples.note: Fa-'a-la has three fathahs: three quick 'a' sounds.
Bi and mi both carry a kasrah; the middle letter carries a sukun (next lesson).
Qul has a dammah; hu has a dammah; wa has a fathah.
Ih-di-naa: a kasrah, a kasrah, a fathah.

cards.q: Which short vowel is a small line BELOW a letter?
How long does a short vowel last?

lessons.title: Sukun
lessons.summary: A letter with a sukun has no vowel of its own. It closes the sound that came before it.
explain: In the Madinah Mushaf the sukun is a small open-headed circle (ۡ) above the letter; many printed books use a plain small circle (ْ). They mean the same thing.
A letter with sukun is pronounced together with the vowelled letter before it: بِسْمِ is bis-mi, not bi-si-mi.
how: Say the vowelled letter, then land lightly on the sukun letter. It is a gentle stop inside the word, with no extra vowel after it.
tips: Think of a sukun as a tiny closed door: the sound stops there for a moment.
mistakes: Adding a hidden vowel after the sukun letter (saying bi-sa-mi).

examples.note: Qul: the lam carries a sukun.
Al-ḥamd: a sukun on the lam, and another on the meem when you stop.
Na'-bu-du: the ayn carries a sukun.
Al-mus-ta-qeem: sukuns on the lam and the sin.

cards.q: What does a sukun do to a letter?
cards.a: It removes the vowel: the letter is pronounced with no vowel of its own, joined to the letter before it.

lessons.title: Shaddah (Doubled Letter)
lessons.summary: A tiny mark shaped like a little 'w' doubles the letter: one half closes the sound before it, the other half opens the sound after it.
explain: A letter with a shaddah is really two identical letters in a row: the first has a sukun, the second has the vowel shown.
So لِلَّهِ is lil-lah: the first lam ends 'lil', the second lam starts 'lah'.
A shaddah makes the letter firm and a touch longer. When the letter is a noon or meem, it also carries a nasal hum, the ghunnah (Level 1).
how: Press the letter firmly once, then release into its vowel. Think 'hold, then open'.
tips: Count the letter twice in your head: lam-lam.
mistakes: Reading a doubled letter as a single, soft one.

examples.note: Lil-lah: a doubled lam.
Iy-yaa-ka: a doubled yaa.
As-sa-mad: the doubled ṣād (the lam before it is silent; see sun letters, Level 4).
Tab-bat: a doubled ba.

cards.q: A letter with a shaddah is pronounced...
cards.a: Twice: a sukun half that closes the previous sound, then a vowelled half that opens the next one.

lessons.title: Tanween
lessons.summary: A doubled mark at the end of a noun adds a light 'n' sound: -an, -in, -un.
explain: Tanween appears only on the LAST letter of a noun. Fathatan (ـً) says -an, kasratan (ـٍ) says -in, dammatan (ـٌ) says -un.
Tanween is a noon sakinah (نْ) that you pronounce but never write. That is why it follows the same four rules as noon sakinah in Level 1.
When you stop on a word, tanween disappears (and fathatan becomes a long 'aa'). You will practise that in Level 6.
how: Say the vowel, then close with a quick, light 'n'.
tips: Tanween is just a short vowel plus an invisible noon.
mistakes: Skipping the final 'n' sound when you continue reading.

examples.note: A-ha-dun: dammatan, but you stop here, so you say 'aḥad'.
Ku-fu-wan: fathatan on the waw.
Khus-rin: kasratan.

cards.a: A light 'n' after the short vowel: -an, -in or -un.

cards.q: Where does tanween appear in a word?
cards.a: Only on the last letter of a noun.

lessons.title: Long Vowels (Alif, Waw, Yaa)
lessons.summary: Alif, waw and yaa can stretch a short vowel into a long one lasting 2 counts.
explain: Alif stretches a fathah: بَا = baa.
An unmarked waw stretches a dammah: بُو = boo.
An unmarked yaa stretches a kasrah: بِي = bee.
This is the natural madd, shown in light blue. It is the foundation of every other kind of madd.
how: Say the short vowel, then keep the same sound going for two counts, steady and relaxed.
tips: Match the vowel before the letter: fathah goes with alif, dammah with waw, kasrah with yaa.
mistakes: Cutting the long vowel short, or stretching it far beyond two counts.

examples.note: A-'oo-dhu (waw), bi-rab-bi (short), an-naa-si (alif).
Yoo-lad: a waw after a dammah.
Iy-yaa-ka (alif) and nas-ta-'een (yaa).
Maa-li-ki (dagger alif), yawm (a different sound), ad-deen (yaa).

cards.q: Which long vowel letter matches a dammah?
Which long vowel letter matches a kasrah?
How long is a natural madd?

lessons.title: Little Letters of the Mushaf
lessons.meaning: Dagger alif, small waw and small yaa
lessons.summary: To save space, the Mushaf writes some long vowels as tiny letters above or below the line.
explain: The dagger alif (ـٰ) is a small upright stroke over a letter. It means a long 'aa' of 2 counts: ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ is ar-raḥ-maa-ni.
The small waw (ۥ) follows a pronoun هُ and stretches it to 'huu': لَهُۥ = lahuu.
The small yaa (ۦ) follows a pronoun هِ and stretches it to 'hee': بِهِۦ = bihee.
All three are natural madd: 2 counts, in light blue. (If a hamza comes right after, the madd gets longer; see Level 3.)
how: Read the tiny letter as if it were a full alif, waw or yaa, and give it two counts.
tips: If you see a tiny letter, you hear a long vowel.
mistakes: Ignoring the tiny letters because they are small.

examples.note: Ar-raḥ-maa-ni: dagger alif.
Maa-liki: dagger alif.
Lahuu: small waw.
Bihee: small yaa.

cards.q: What does a dagger alif (ـٰ) mean?
What does the small waw (ۥ) after a pronoun ه do?
cards.a: It stretches 'hu' into 'huu' for 2 counts (between two vowelled letters).
